entries.title: Germany news: Friedrich Merz calls for global free trade alliance during Asia trip
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's comments come at the end of his multi-day tour. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier is set to hold talks with Xi Jinping. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz calls for global free trade alliance in Asia

October 30, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's comments come at the end of his multi-day tour. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier is set to hold talks with Xi Jinping. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz is ending his multi-day trip to Asia
  • President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping

Here are the leading headlines from Germany on Friday, October 30:

Skip next section Merz pushes for new free trade network

Merz pushes for new free trade network

Chancellor Merz has again called for a global network of countries with a commitment to free trade based on international rules.

His comments came while in South Korea on the final day of his four-day trip to Asia. He was speaking at the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," he said.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions," Merz added.

The chancellor had made a similar call in Singapore and Japan.

"German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region," South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook said at Thursday's conference.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany seeks new head of state

IN DEPTH: Germany seeks new head of state

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Read DW's full report on who may be the next German president.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is closing off his four-day trip to Asia, while President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is separately in China, where he is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Keep reading for the latest updates from Germany.

entries.title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado says US backs 2027 election
entries.summary: The return of Maria Corina Machado, who says Trump opened the "floodgate to freedom" for Venezuela, presents a challenge for Washington as Trump has also backed interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
entries.content:
Venezuela

Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado says US backs 2027 election

October 30, 2026

The return of Maria Corina Machado, who says Trump opened the "floodgate to freedom" for Venezuela, presents a challenge for Washington as Trump has also backed interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.

Calling the transition to democracy "irreversible," Machado said, "US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes ​presidential elections in 2027."

"The date of the election is the date of liberation," Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.

Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Shortly before Machado's public statements, Rodriguez announced that there "will be elections" in Venezuela, without specifying a date.

Machado says Trump helped open 'floodgate to freedom'

Machado, who famously "presented" US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to "the floodgate to freedom" being opened in Venezuela.

The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.

Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.

"This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," she said.

At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.

US caught in a bind

Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.

Machado's recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.

entries.title: Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
entries.summary: The weedkiller Roundup has been accused of being carcinogenic to humans despite no warning on its label. Bayer is seeking to settle tens of thousands of further cases.
entries.content:
October 30, 2026

The weedkiller Roundup has been accused of being carcinogenic to humans despite no warning on its label. Bayer is seeking to settle tens of thousands of further cases.

The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.

The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.

Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.

What is the complaint against Roundup?

Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.

The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.

Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably ​dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.

The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.

What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?

The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.

"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement. 

"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.

The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."

The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

entries.title: Binance crypto platform suspends trades amid suspected hack
entries.summary: The platform suspended some trading while crypto companies froze billions in their respective currencies. The full extent of the possible hack was not yet clear.
entries.content:
October 30, 2026

The platform suspended some trading while crypto companies froze billions in their respective currencies. The full extent of the possible hack was not yet clear.

The world's largest cryptocurrency platform, Binance, confirmed on Thursday that it was investigating a potential security breach that resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact.

Analysts said the breach could amount to the largest-ever crypto heist

"It does look like a hack on Binance," said former company chief Changpeng Zhao, who remains a major shareholder.

Binance said it worked to freeze the affected assets and that it had located about $3 billion so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion.

"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.

Some $3 billion (€2.7 billion) had been frozen in response to the suspected hack.

Binance 'reviewing' possible hack

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the company statement said.

"Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote. "We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."

The company, which is the world's largest platform in terms of daily crypto trading volume, suspended trading on certain products while the freezing came from cryptocurrency companies using the platform.

Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.

Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?

The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.

Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.

entries.title: Israeli election: Netanyahu, main rival fall short of majority after all votes counted
entries.summary: With all the votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc finished ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc. But as neither grouping won a majority, tough coalition talks are ahead. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Majority remains elusive after final count

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 30, 2026

With all the votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc finished ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc. But as neither grouping won a majority, tough coalition talks are ahead. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
  • The final vote count showed Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc finished with 53 seats
  • The anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, claimed 48 seats
  • At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
  • As neither party won an outright majority, difficult coalition talks are expected in the weeks ahead

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election.

Skip next section Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins

Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins

Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.

On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.

However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.

The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.

Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.

He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.

It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.

Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.

Skip next section Final count released

Final count released

The final count of ballots from Tuesday's vote has been released by Israel's Central Election Committee.

Netanyahu's bloc with a total of 53 seats

  • Likud - 27
  • UTJ - 7
  • Otzma Yehudit - 7
  • Shas - 6
  • RZP - 6

Eisenkot's bloc with a total of 48 seats

  • Yashar - 21
  • B'Yachad - 12
  • The Democrats - 8
  • Yisrael Beytenu - 7

The Arab Israeli parties with a total of 19 seats

  • Joint List - 11
  • Ra'am - 8

Skip next section READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims

READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims. 

Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”

A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.

Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here. 

Skip next section Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon

Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon

With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.

  • Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
  • Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
  • Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
  • Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
  • Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
  • Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
  • Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
  • The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
  • Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
  • "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.

Skip next section Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.

That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.

The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.

Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.

The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.

Skip next section Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.

Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.

According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.

This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.

The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.

Skip next section UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law. 

"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.

"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."

Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.

He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."

Skip next section 'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.

"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."

Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.

"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.

Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.

Skip next section WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.

Some small positives may be possible though.

Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.

Skip next section GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

Skip next section Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.

These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.

This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.

Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.

Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.

If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.

Skip next section President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.

"I will receive  the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions." 

Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.

"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments. 

Skip next section Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.

The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.

Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.

The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.

The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.

The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.

Skip next section Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu

Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu

The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.

"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.

"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."

After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.

Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."

However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.

entries.title: Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
entries.summary: Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.

Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.

Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.

Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.

He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.

"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.

"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."

Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

Two Grand Slams in 2026

Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.

The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.

Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

entries.title: 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86
entries.summary: The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

In love with Shakespeare

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

'Star Trek' offer from Hollywood

In the same year, Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

Adventures in the universe

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time.



At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center. 

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

A short-lived retirement

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

Translated from German by Sarah Hucal.

entries.title: Justice for Maya women in Guatemala, girls back in school in India, restored land in Mali: The UN has named its 2026 SDG Action Award winners
entries.summary: Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

Champions of indigenous women's rights in Guatemala, girls' education in India, and restored farmland in Mali all featured among the winners of UN's SDG Action Awards.

A legal aid group for Indigenous women in Guatemala, a movement of village mothers in rural India, and a Malian entrepreneur who restores farmland have won this year's UN SDG Action Awards.

The winners were announced at the ninth Heroes of Tomorrow awards ceremony in Rome, Italy, run by the UN SDG Action Campaign. They were chosen from more than 7,000 entries from 190 countries.

Nine finalists were shortlisted for three categories: resilience, creativity and changemaker.

Justice for Maya women

The Resilience Award went to the Women's Justice Initiative. Many indigenous women in Guatemala face high rates of violence, poverty and discrimination, made worse by language barriers and a lack of access to information. The initiative helps women and girls get access to justice and lead change in their communities. According to the organization, more than 16,000 women and girls have participated.

"I accept the UN SDG Action Award in the honour of the Maya Kaqchikel women and girls in Guatemala who are building a more just future for their communities. Ending violence against women requires all of us. Only together, we can build a future where every woman and girl lives with dignity and realizes her full potential," said Viviana Patal, the initiative's legal director.

Keeping girls in school in India

The Creativity Award was given to Mothers of Courage, a grassroots campaign that aims to keep girls in education in rural India. Its organizers say more than 1.2 million people have joined and pledged to keep their daughters in education and to prevent early marriage.

"This award today belongs to all the mothers in those villages, all the women leaders, who are working hard to change the destinies of their daughters and their daughters-in-law," said Khushboo Awasthi, Mothers of Courage's chief curator.

"Together, let's create a world where no girl ever has to negotiate for her right to dream and to aspire and to thrive."

Trees and livelihoods in Mali

The Changemaker Award when to Malian entrepreneur Rokiatou Traore. Her organization, Herou Alliance, helps women and small farmers bring worn-out land back to life by planting trees alongside their crops. The trees also help farmers generate extra revenue, allowing them to sell products from moringa and other valuable trees.

"Receiving this award means a lot to me. It is a reminder of why I started this journey," said Traore. "I invite you all to join us, to plant more trees, to empower more women, and above all, to create a future full of opportunities for communities for today and for future generations."

The UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women and Girls received an honorable mention. Speaking about the award, President of the Organization of Women's Freedom in Iraq Jannat Al Ghezi paid a tearful tribute to its founder Yanar Mohammed, who was assassinated outside her home in Baghdad in March.

'Be that change'

UN Assistant Secretary-General Michelle Muschett said the finalists "remind us that the future is something we create together and that each of us has the power to help shape it and open doors for the next generations."

"When they tell you that one person cannot make a difference, prove them wrong," UN SDG Action Campaign Director Marina Ponti told the audience. "Change has always begun with people who refused to accept that the world could not be different. So be courageous. Be persistent. Be that change."

How are the awards organized?

A panel of 20 judges from UN leadership, government, civil society, the arts, business and youth activism chose the winners. They included UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo, Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar, and Otto Group Vice President Tobias Wollermann.

The awards are run by the UN SDG Action Campaign, a special initiative of the UN Secretary-General. The campaign supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, 17 targets adopted by member states that cover areas including poverty, hunger, education, gender equality and climate protection.

The awards are supported by Italy's Foreign Ministry and Germany's Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Editor's Note: DW Director General Barbara Massing was a member of the 20-person jury panel.

entries.title: Berlin's Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview
entries.summary: Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin's Left leader Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview

October 29, 2026

Left candidate Elif Eralp has sparked controversy after Der Speigel reported she was advised against mentioning a pro-Palestinian activist for fear of reprisals against her family.

Elif Eralp, the candidate on course to become the next mayor of Berlin, sparked controversy on Thursday after having unintentionally aired personal security fears that appeared to be linked to pro-Palestinian activists in the city.

The controversy came about based on internal remarks that were part of her interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel.

Eralp, whose Left Party (Die Linke) came out on top in local elections in Berlin last month, appeared to suggest in remarks made during an internal authorization process for an interview that she gave to Der Spiegel that she couldn't make references to a particular pro-Palestinian activist out of fear for her own safety.

"I can't put myself and my family in danger for Der Spiegel," the magazine cites her as having written in a Word Document edit, which was inadvertently sent back to the reporters.

"What do we do now? Cancel the whole interview?" she is cited as having asked her press officer and other party colleagues, while stating in another remark, "I should never have agreed to this interview."

Elif Eralp under pressure to clearly label out threats she sees

In the Der Spiegel interview, which was conducted on Monday in Eralp's office in Berlin's House of Representatives, the 45-year-old was asked about allegations of antisemitism that have been leveled at members of her socialist party.

Those accusations came about after at least two instances where people with questionable backgrounds showed up to celebrate after Eralp's party won elections in the city state last month.

For instance, the Left Party election celebration in the Berlin district of Neukölln was attended by a controversial pro-Palestinian activist associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is classified as a terrorist organization by the European Union.

In the past, Ibrahim Ibrahim has described Yahya Sinwar, the former head of Hamas in Gaza, widely regarded as the mastermind behind the deadly terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as a "martyr" and a "hero." He has since rejected accusations of antisemitism and of supporting terrorism or Hamas.

Asked by Der Spiegel whether she was referring to the Ibrahim incident, Eralp initially responded with a "yes." But she later returned the interview transcript to the magazine with the question crossed out and the comment regarding her and her family's safety.

In Germany, it is standard practice for an interviewee to review and approve direct quotations with media outlets before the interview is published.

In notes included in the approved version of the transcript, which Der Spiegel believes were left in by accident, Eralp wrote that Berlin police had previously advised her not to comment on specific individuals.

Der Spiegel on why it published the notes

That Eralp chose to conceal her concerns publicly led some politicians to ask whether she was the right person to be the mayor of Berlin.

Der Spiegel wrote in its story:

"There were reasons not to publish – Eralp's security concerns first and foremost," the magazine wrote. "But the political importance of her notes outweighed them. Der Spiegel believes that the public should know."

It added that the story begs the question: "Can a woman who is too scared to name a terrorist sympathizer in an interview be responsible for the security of all Berliners?"

SPD, Greens also weigh in

Rival politicians weighed in, including from the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, with whom the Left Party is due to conduct coalition talks in Berlin next month.

"I would advise my party to distance itself from an alliance with the Left Party," said the SPD's Karl Lauterbach, who rose to prominence as Germany's health minister during the Covid-19 pandemic.

"Further talks about a coalition with this party should be out of the question for any social democrat," added SPD internal affairs spokesman Sebastian Fiedler.

Katharina Dröge, the leader of the Green Party's parliamentary grouping, asked in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, "Will [Eralp] continue to let herself be influenced by those in her own ranks who are close to criminal groups and who tolerate threats and intimidation towards their own lead candidate? Or will she manage to give a clear and tough response?"

The chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, warned: "The SPD and the Greens have a duty not to hand governmental responsibility for Berlin and for the security of the Jewish community to the Left Party" and claimed the story showed that "the Left Party is incapable of distancing itself from terrorist sympathizers and antisemites."

Eralp issues tough response, hits out at critics

Eralp hit back later on Thursday, slamming a "truly toxic debate," vowing not to be intimidated and promising a tough stance "against organized crime, against organizations that glorify violence, against violence, against terror."

She said she wouldn't comment on the specifics of the Der Spiegel story but insisted that she would "ensure the security of all Berliners."

Eralp also received backing from the vice-president of the German parliament and veteran Left Party colleague Bodo Ramelow, who criticized the Der Spiegel story as "more than questionable."

He said the reporting "targeted a person who feels vulnerable and made them even more vulnerable." He said internal communications had been used to depict the "anachronistic cliché" of a "weak woman."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Iraq: Life sentences for 3 French 'Islamic State' suspects
entries.summary: The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.
entries.content:
October 29, 2026

The three were among 47 French "Islamic State" suspects transferred from Syrian detention. So far, ten French nationals have received prison terms after being convicted of belonging to the group.

Three French nationals on Thursday received sentences of life imprisonment in Iraq after being convicted of joining the so-called "Islamic State" terror group.

The criminal court in Baghdad sentence Charly S., Kamal M, and Amir A. to life terms in prison which amounts to 20 years of imprisonment in Iraq.

What more do we know?

The trio were found guilty of "the crime of joining the terrorist Islamic State organisation and of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror," an AFP correspondent said.

Tuesday saw another six French nationals from the same group sentenced to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years for belonging ​to the Islamist militant group.

All of the French nationals sentenced thus far belong to a group of 47 French nationals who were transferred from detention in Syria last year.

The 'Islamic State's' years of terror in Syria and Iraq

The militant group carried out a campaign of terror as it sought to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate in Iraq and Syria from 2014 under its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.

Thousands of foreign nationals from across the world joined the group, which carried out mass executions and other atrocities, many of them filmed and shared on social media platforms.

Among its most heinous crimes was the capture and killing of thousands of Yazidis in Iraq’s northern Sinjar region. Many Yazidi women and children were forced into sexual slavery and other forms of enslavement.

In 2014, IS also captured and killed hundreds of Iraqi military cadets at Camp Speicher in Iraq's Tikrit in 2014, much of the massacre filmed and shared on social media.

The terror group also carried out a series of executions of Western journalists and aid workers in highly choreographed videos as part of its media campaign.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and along with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces would go on to ultimately defeat the group territorially in Syria two years later.

The remaining fighters were eventually cornered and defeated in Baghouz in Syria's eastern Deir Ezzor, near the Iraqi border in March, 2019.
